description.narrative: The Fair, Green and Global Alliance (FGG) aims to increase the power and decision-making influence of organised, mobilised and informed civil society, especially women, to advance fair and green trade and value chains. FGG believes that poverty, inequality and exclusion are caused by power asymmetries. We see the unprecedented power of capital over people and planet as the primary obstacle impeding realisation of fair and green trade and value chains. The FGG programme focuses on recalibrating power within the global architecture of trade and value chains by amplifying the voices of targeted rights-holders – small producers and traders, workers, fishers, rural and Indigenous peoples, religious and ethnic minorities, and migrants, especially the women and youth among them – who are practising, claiming or defending human rights and fair and green economic practices, and/or whose rights are being ignored, threatened or violated by corporations and/or governments. We aim to transform social relations so that these rights-holders’ voices are heard and heeded. FGG’s eight members (ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie/Friends of the Earth International/Friends of the Earth Europe, Samdhana Institute, SOMO and the Transnational Institute) cooperate with some 1000+ partners and allies in our many worldwide networks to strengthen collective capacities to advance a common vision of fair and green trade and value chains.

2023 At least 1 new target country rejects joining the ECT, as the agreement undermines the implementation of the Paris Climate Agreement.

Between July and December 2022, seven EU member states (Poland, Spain, Netherlands, France, Germany, Slovenia and Luxembourg) announced their intention to withdraw from the ECT. These decisions were informed by the conclusions that the ECT, even after being modernized, continues to pose great risks for climate policies. Several landmark arbitration cases have proved that the ECT can be used for fossil fuel investors to claim compensation for climate or environmental measures. CSOs have been warning for the climate impact of the ECT for several years, and have criticized the modernization process for being too unambitious, calling for a termination of the ECT instead. In addition, international institutions like the IPCC, UN and IMF have warned for the ECT impacts on climate policy. The outcome is important, making withdrawal or termination of international agreements that protect the interests of the fossil fuel industry a viable and legitimate political strategy. In November 2022, 4 EU member states (Spain, France, Germany, Netherlands) formed a blocking minority in the Council in a vote on adopting a common EU position on the modernization of the ECT. This meant that the Council could not adopt such a position, leading to a postponement of the ECT vote on the modernization to April 2023. Shortly after, the European Parliament adopted a resolution calling for a coordinated EU withdrawal from the ECT. Together, this means that the EU cannot adopt the modernized ECT, but cannot stay within the existing ECT (because it is incompatible with EU law), so the only option going forward is that the EU leaves the ECT. These events followed efforts by a network of European CSOs, including SOMO, working on the ECT and warning for the impacts on climate policy. In November 2022, the Dutch court ruled that the Dutch government will not have to pay damages to energy giants RWE and Uniper. The energy companies had filed claims of EUR 1.4 billion and EUR 1 billion respectively against the Dutch state, claiming the ban on coal-fired power generation by 2030 was a form of expropriation. The court held that the coal ban does not unlawfully infringe on property rights and that it was foreseeable to the owners of the coal-fired power plants. In the past years, SOMO and other FGG members have consistently worked on informing policymakers as well as the general public about the possibility and chilling effect of such claims for legislation. This may have contributed to the result of this ruling. This ruling is an important victory for the climate and the phase-out of fossil fuels. The ruling prevents polluting companies that knowingly invest in climate-disrupting activities from evading responsibility. The Mongolian public prosecutor’s office changed their position from being intent on prosecuting a human rights defender for their work, to stopping their investigation in late 2022/early 2023. SOMO and various civil society allies engaged with various states and intergovernmental organisations to use their leverage with Mongolia to safeguard the country’s civic space.

comment.narrative:
2022 By end of 2022, we think it is realistic to have advanced to deeper support of the recommendations in 6 cases. In this we see the greatest potential to be on energy transition recommendations.
We expect key government actors in EU to support recommendations on changes to the Energy Charter Treaty. We expect key government actors in Latin America to support recommendations on a more just approach to energy transition and use of natural resources.
2023 Parliamentarians in at least 2 countries call for the country not to ratify the ECT and 2 governmental actors in 2 countries call for companies to remediate environmental and social damage before divesting from fossil fuels.

(1) Together with many other CSOs across Europe, SOMO has contributed to raising public awareness about the negative impact of the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT) and its investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) mechanism on energy transition and climate action. In February 2021, the European Commission published its proposal to phase out fossil fuel protection under the ECT. Current ECT reform negotiations are advancing very slowly, with some non-EU countries (1) objecting to the EU proposal. In response, Spain, France, Poland, Luxembourg, Greece, Latvia, Hungary and Cyprus are all demanding a legal assessment of a coordinated EU withdrawal from the ECT in absence of a consensus on the ECT reform. The European Commission has set June 2022 as a deadline before which a meaningful reform should be delivered. Meanwhile, in September 2021 the European Court of Justice found in the landmark Komstroy ruling that intra-EU arbitration under the ECT is incompatible with EU law, meaning that the ECT should no longer be available for disputes involving an EU investor and an EU member state. This puts even more pressure on the European Commission and EU member states to either negotiate a waiver for intra-EU disputes (unlikely to receive support from non-EU countries) or withdraw from the ECT.
(1) In June 2021, recommendations made by SOMO and other civil society groups in relation to a complaint mechanism to address non-compliance with sustainable development provisions under EU free trade agreements were taken up by the Dutch government (1) in its official position. This was the result of successful coordinated advocacy. Between February and April 2021, SOMO participated in three meetings organised by the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Social Economic Council (SER) on the newly created Single Entry Point as an internal complaint mechanism for CSOs to address non-compliance with sustainable development provisions under EU free trade agreements. Together with CNV, FNV, Milieudefensie, VCP and Handel Anders, SOMO made recommendations, including on: pre-notification support when filing a complaint; type of information required to substantiate a complaint; establishing transparency and concrete timelines; and clarifying the relationship between the Domestic Advisory Group established under EU Free Trade Agreements and the SEP.
(1) On 15 October 2021, the tribunal at the International Centre for Settlement of investment disputes (ICSID) (1) in the RWE (a German multinational energy company) vs Netherlands case agreed to apply the UNCITRAL Transparency Rules. This means that both the Dutch state, even though the Netherlands has not formally ratified those rules, and RWE commit - in principle - to open hearings, access to documents and to allow third parties to submit an amicus curiae brief. This decision has been informed by SOMO, FGG partners TNI and Milieudefensie, and others, calling for transparency in this case and to allow the public scrutiny and participation, particularly in parliamentary questions in February 2021, and sets an important precedent for future climate policy-related arbitration cases.

(1) In July 2021, the Independent Complaints Mechanism (ICM) associated with EU Development Finance Institutions (DFIs), found a complaint involving a Financial Intermediary (FI) eligible. This is a ground-breaking change in practice by this non-judicial grievance mechanism. Development banks are increasingly outsourcing their lending to commercial banks and other financial institutions, which then invest it onward, often with little oversight. The eligibility decision set an important precedent for communities affected by other EU DFI funding via FIs to seek accountability before the ICM upon the fulfilment of certain technical conditions. The case complaint that led to the decision alleges that EU DFIs failed to ensure that FirstRand Bank, an FI, had adequate Environmental and Social risk management systems in place to monitor its own high-risk clients and, specifically, the performances of the New Liberty Gold Mine that FirstRand financed. SOMO supported capacity building of two NGOs involved in the case to enable them to file a complaint to the ICM.
(13) OECD Watch's second evaluation of NCPs helped prompt 13 of them to improve their rules of procedure or structure to better facilitate access to remedy and civil society input. This is a landmark decision after years of campaigning by civil society and others. The UN Tax Convention will move global decision-making on tax to the UN rather than the wealthy countries in the OECD. This can lead to policy and resolutions that better favour the rights of LLICs. SOMO and TJNL have for years called for better representation of the Global South in international policy-making regarding tax. The decision gives Indigenous communities in the oil fields of the Peruvian Amazon a path for seeking remediation from Pluspetrol for the polluted soil and waterways that have harmed the communities’ health and way of life.
(1) In her 2021 State of the Union Address on 25 September 2021, EU President von der Leyen (1) said the EU will propose a ban on products made by forced labour. This commitment reflects years of work by civil society groups including SOMO. Reports about forced labour, including the report by Arisa and SOMO on forced labour in the textile and garment industry in Tamil Nadu, have demonstrated that voluntary initiatives and corporate self-regulation are insufficient in eliminating forced labour from global supply chains and that robust regulation at the EU level is essential.
(1) The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) (1) issued a letter confirming OECD Watch and BankTrack's view that nominee shareholding creates a business relationship, making financial institutions responsible for adverse impacts of the company for which it provides such services (i.e., nominee shareholders). The initiative to see an OHCHR statement on this matter followed a statement by the Swiss NCP (the complaints mechanism linked to the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises) that nominee shareholding services of a financial institution do not create a business relationship that would the financial institution responsible for adverse impacts of the company for which it provides those services. OECD Watch and SOMO disagreed, and joined partner BankTrack in asking OHCHR to provide a view. This OHCHR statement helps pave the way for NCP complaints, and possibly judicial complaints, against financial institutions for their connection to adverse impacts via nominee shareholding services.
(2) Two NCPs issued final statements in NCP complaints confirming that companies breached the OECD Guidelines, thereby allowing victims some element of remedy, and clarifying responsible business conduct standards for MNEs. These findings help teach companies the meaning of the correct application of the Guidelines, and provide a form of recognition and remedy to impacted people. OECD Watch, hosted by SOMO, advised and supported the complainants.
(1) The coalition agreement between D66, CDA and VVD, which was published on 15 December 2021, included the introduction of Dutch due diligence legislation. This means that the Dutch government (1) will no longer tolerate abuses in the global value chains of companies, e.g. labour rights abuses, environmental pollution and child labour. The MVO Platform, hosted by SOMO, along with other Dutch civil society groups including SOMO, has been working towards this for years, and engaged in strategic advocacy in 2021 to promote action at the Dutch and EU levels on due diligence.
(1) In June 2021, FMO issued its Position Statement on Phasing Out Fossil Fuels for Direct Investments (Fossil Fuel Statement). This follows extensive advocacy by SOMO, Both ENDS and others. Following on its 2016 policy commitment on coal mining and power generation, this Position Statement partially complements the bank’s approach to climate change issues by committing to reduce its direct exposure to the oil and gas industries. For example, the Statement restricts FMO’s direct financing of fossil fuels’ exploration, extraction, and transportation, as well as oil-based power generation and transmission lines, amongst others. In February 2022, the European Commission has published its proposal for a Directive on corporate sustainability due diligence (CSDDD), which, after revision, could represent a landmark step forward in the direction of minimising the negative impacts of businesses on workers, communities and the environment worldwide, and advancing corporate accountability and justice. The European Coalition for Corporate Justice (ECCJ), of which SOMO is a board member and active participant in the working group focusing on due diligence legislation, has been advocating strongly for the Directive and improvements to the current draft.
In its coalition agreement, published January 2022, the Dutch government agreed to develop due diligence legislation to promote for responsible business conduct by companies abroad.
Over 65 companies and 60 civil society organisations, including SOMO, ActionAid, Both ENDS, SKC, and trade unions have been campaigning for due diligence legislation through the Sustainable and Responsible Business Conduct Initiative (IDVO.org), which is facilitated by the MVO Platform of which a number of FGG organisations are also member. In June 2022 the OECD has started a process to go through targeted updates to the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, which could potentially strengthen responsible business conduct standards regarding human rights defenders, land rights, corporate tax practices, the environment and climate change, and the digital economy, among other issues – as well as enhance access to remedy. OECD Watch, hosted by SOMO, is the official stakeholder to the OECD for this issue and has been actively collecting CSO input into the revision process. On 1 November 2022, six Dutch political parties (ChristenUnie, D66, PvdA, GroenLinks, SP, Volt) have formally submitted their Bill on Responsible and Sustainable International Business Conduct to the Dutch House of Representatives, in an effort to oblige enterprises to conduct business with respect for human rights, the environment, and the climate in accordance with the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. The Dutch government agreed to review this legislative proposal before continuing with its own legislative proposal. Four key CSO recommendations for strengthening batteries regulations were endorsed by the European Parliament, Commission and Council during the trilogue negotiations as shown by the Draft Agreement reached on November, 2022, and the final compromise text published on 18 of January, 2023. Throughout 2022, SOMO and other CSOs such as ActionAid, Clean Clothes Campaign, and Milieudefensie, sent several joint statements and letters with recommendations for strengthening batteries regulation to the European union co-legislators. In December 2022, the European Council has adopted its negotiating position ('general approach') on the corporate sustainability due diligence directive (CSDDD). Although the Council is generally supportive of the directive, civil society is disappointed with the Council's lack of ambition. A good directive could represent a landmark step forward in the direction of minimising the negative impacts of businesses on workers, communities and the environment worldwide, and advancing corporate accountability and justice.
The European Coalition for Corporate Justice (ECCJ), of which SOMO is a board member and active participant in the working group focusing on due diligence legislation, has been advocating strongly for the Directive and improvements to the current draft. In October 2022, FMO's Independent Complaints Mechanism (ICM) released its final report and confirmed that the Barro Blanco hydropower project that was financed by FMO and DEG remained in non-compliance with the banks’ social and environmental safeguards and issued recommendations to address the outstanding non-compliances, including recommending the banks issue a public apology and provide compensation to the affected communities as a basis for a responsible divestment. SOMO supported and coordinated with CSO group M10 about specific issues raised by the ICM. In May 2022, the Dutch Social and Economic Council (SER) announced a two-year project which has the objective to improve corporate practice with regard to meaningful stakeholder engagement. Experience within sectoral IRBC (International Responsible Business Conduct) agreements, facilitated by the SER, led the SER to conclude that business performs very poorly when it comes to engaging meaningfully with stakeholders. The SER will develop guidance for companies to engage with stakeholders and rights holders in a meaningful manner. SOMO has raised the importance of meaningful stakeholder engagement as an essential element of corporate human rights due diligence procedures (in its reports, in bilateral conversations with SER representatives) and has pointed out corporate failure to engage meaningfully with civil society stakeholders (notably, in the context of the complaint against C&A). In March 2022, the European Parliament approved Digital Markets Act (DMA) text that includes important civil society asks, such as expanding the types of mergers that need to be notified to competition authorities and the removal of the term ‘digital’ data from the text on merger notification. SOMO held advocacy meetings in the Netherlands and Brussels with representatives of the governments of Germany, Luxembourg, Estonia and Denmark and ran a mini social media campaign targeting key officials and parliamentarians, the DMA rapporteur for the European Parliament (who reacted to a SOMO post) and several French government officials involved in the DMA. Limiting the notification of mergers and acquisitions to those carried out between digital companies or involving ‘digital’ data risked excluding important mergers, and could have led to increased acquisition of data by technology companies. Improving the Digital Markets Act contributes to defending civic space by reducing the control and influence of Big Tech platforms. In October 2022 Dutch minister Schreinemacher made a public statement that she wants a thorough revision of the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. The Netherlands supports explicitly mentioning the safety of human rights defenders in the OECD Guidelines, as is in line with the Dutch human rights policy.

comment.narrative:
2022 SOMO organises learning sessions on organisational as well as on team level. On organisational level, SOMO regularly reflects on current issues, e.g. via presentations during weekly stand-ups or sessions on more cross-cutting issues such as HRD protection, gender or conflict sensitivity, taking into account the learnings from the specific projects. More recently we started also reflecting on moral dilemmas.
On team level, SOMO’s project teams evaluate their projects at least once a year during outcome harvesting sessions. In these sessions the teams reflect on what their plans were and compare to what has actually been achieved. Wherever we find disparities the team collectively offers suggestions as to why these disparities occurred, what we can learn from them and how we can apply lessons learned in future endeavours. These conversations however do not only take place in scheduled learning sessions but also take place informally during team meetings or correspondence with partner organisations.
Going beyond our own organisation, we strive to have yearly reflection meetings with all our partner organisations in which we evaluate and reflect more broadly on our work taking learned lessons of previous work into account. Furthermore, we expect to host/co-host learning sessions on tech monopolies, stranded liabilities and value chain analysis. description.narrative: lines of work in which FGG members and partners build upon gender analysis and incorporate gender justice in their strategy

comment.narrative:
2022 Work we do under FGG is increasingly based on a gender analysis. In 2022, we will develop or update our gender analysis for our work on public services and ISDS, specifically in the ECT. Also, our advocacy for a Binding Treaty, we build on a gender analysis. Whereas our work on public services already has a strong gender justice component, integration of a gender lens for our work on ISDS will be a priority in the coming year. We will work and learn together with partners from several Latin American and Asian countries.
The main elements will be: 1. Building a gender analysis into research and recommendations, so research is not gender blind. This will be done with partners (joint research). 2. Including gender-equity “asks” into advocacy on climate justice and garments, as well as within wider policy agendas such as UN Treaty, Due Diligence Laws.
Our objectives can be stated as: 1. Increase awareness of, and bring a more sophisticated analysis to bear on the gendered value chain, exposing how value is extracted in certain sectors based on exploitation of women’s labour, reinforcing gender inequality 2. Ensure that a fair and just energy transition includes gender equality as a key element of what constitutes “just” transition. Specifically, the rights, and the political and economic situation of women, which were side-lined and undermined by the fossil fuel sector are brought front and centre of energy transition.
We expect to work with partners in: Nigeria, Colombia, Peru, Indonesia, Philippines, Argentina, DRC (over the five years). In 2022 the work will only be starting so targets do not reflect work in all these countries
2023 SOMO is in a process of integrating gender analysis into work more systematically, both for research and subsequent advocacy. In our work on garments (textile and leather) and climate justice in particular, in 2023 we and our partners expect to have a deeper engagement on the gender equity dimensions of the work. As noted previously, much of our work on gender equality is currently focused on the research and analysis, and less so on advocacy. However, as we and our partners develop more robust gender and intersectional analysis and develop more gender-aware recommendations in our research, the advocacy dimension of the work will increase. We would expect to increase advocacy work on gender justice in 2024 and 2025.

description.narrative: strengthened capacities
# targeted civil society actors that lobby and advocate for improved policies and practices in trade and value chains and advance fair and green practices based on capacities mutually developed

comment.narrative:
2022 Throughout 2022, we aim for 6 civil society actors to lobby and advocate for improvements and revisions to trade and investment agreements. This includes: work with CSOs in North Africa on trade deals with the EU which undermine communities’ rights to land; work with Indonesian CSOs on labour rights and trade; and work with CSOs in Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa on transition mineral supply chains. The focus will be on joint re-search and analysis, joint strategizing on advocacy across value chains and training.
2023 In 2023, we aim for 25 civil society actors from countries in Asia, Latin America, Africa and Europe (including Columbia, Mozambique, Nigeria, South Africa, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, Philippines) to lobby and advocate for a socially responsible battery supply chain, responsible divestment from fossil fuels, remedying human rights abuse in the manganese mining sector, and for key improvements in the revision of the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. They will do so with enhanced advocacy, research and networking capacities, strengthened through mutual capacity development activities including research and knowledge building support as well as network facilitation.

(1) SOMO led a team of NGOs to build the Community Resource Exchange (CRE), a platform where civil society actors working with victims of corporate abuse can find resources and information to help them get access to remedies. The CRE was launched in 2021, established three international focal points (in Latin America, Africa, and Eastern Europe respectively). CRE was able , in its first year, to support tens of civil society groups and communities around the world with micro-grants and partnerships aims at securing justice. The initial seed funding for the CRE platform came from Wellspring, but SOMO has developed the CRE work under the Power of Voices program. The platform promotes mutual capacity building between different CSOs and from community to community.
(2) In early 2021, SOMO helped to build the capacity of two West African CSOs on how to file complaints to the ICM, which the EU Development Finance Institutions (DFIs) had established to resolve grievances related to alleged breaches of the EU DFIs’ own social and environmental policy safeguards. Following a series of workshops that local NGO partners conducted with the affected villagers, communities made the informed decision to file a dispute-resolution complaint to the ICM in February 2021. Throughout the second quarter of 2021, SOMO and NGO partners engaged extensively with the ICM to influence their eligibility assessment on this case. The case represents the first ever complaint before the ICM that, rather than alleging the use of banks’ funds in specific harmful projects, focuses on the responsibilities that EU DFIs bear when investing in financial intermediaries (FIs).
(5) SOMO collaborated with five South American and international trade unions, whose capacities were strengthened through the development of the report ‘Responsible disengagement from coal as part of a just transition’ written by SOMO. The report helped the trade unions in their lobby and advocacy towards the coal mining companies and put pressure on them to take responsibility towards workers. SOMO also benefited from the input provided by the unions on the particular concerns of workers and unions, which led to a stronger and more focused report. The report also takes account of gender issues and calls for deeper analysis on the implications of mine closure on women and indigenous peoples.
(2) SOMO successfully built the capacity of a Soutch Asian partner NGO, and a grass-root organization, representing the affected communities in South Asia to navigate the World Bank’s Inspection Panel system. The case involves people adversely affected by the construction of a dry port in the region, a key component of a World Bank-funded Trade and Transport Project. In 2020, SOMO supported the affected people to file a complaint to the World Bank’s Inspection Panel, raising instances of non-compliance with the World Bank’s Safeguard Policies on indigenous peoples’ rights, the consultation process, and cultural rights amongst others. When the Inspection Panel process failed to move forward in a timely manner SOMO’s helped local partners to identify relevant pressure points within the World Bank’s management structure. Following the delivery of letters to all the executive directors, community representatives were able to ensure direct lines of communication with key constituencies of the Bank’s board and to elaborate convincing arguments that led these constituencies to commit to use their leverage in trying to resume the complaint process. In October the Inspection Panel finally informed the complainants about their plan to travel to Nepal in order to finalize the complaint’s admissibility phase. We are awaiting further developments on the complaint in 2022.
(1) OECD Watch members successfully influenced the OECD’s stocktaking exercise on the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. Many civil society issues and recommendations were reflected in the process. This work is a critical milestone in our efforts to secure important reform of the Guidelines.OECD Watch successfully encouraged the OECD to hold a public consultation for the stocktaking. OECD Watch then supported civil society to participate extensively in the public consultation and provided numerous updates, and a template letter to encourage and support CSOs' submissions to the consultation. This was fruitful: more than half of all submissions received were from civil society. The stocktaking reports were then updated by the OECD, following input from OECD Watch and (via OECD Watch's support) other civil society, to reflect detailed analysis on gaps relating to corporate standards, as well as access to remedy via National Contact Points (NCP) for the OECD Guidelines, and suggesting need to improve both the corporate standards and NCPs. SOMO is the host of OECD Watch, whose members are diverse and include and/or represent civil society from LLMUMICs.
(2) Throughout 2021, SOMO built capacities of a South American CSO and grass root organisation to engage with the FMO staff and grievance redress mechanism. In April 2021, FMO, the lead project financier, unexpectedly announced the anticipated repayment of their multimillion loan meaning that the bank’s involvement in the project in question would terminate by the end of 2021. Affected communities raised concerns about this unexpected development, particularly about the lack of clarity on how the bank’s exit would affect the long-standing ICM-led compliance review process through which they expected to obtain accountability for the harms suffered. Throughout the second and third quarter of 2021, SOMO and Both Ends supported community representatives in their quest for clarifications. After FMO made clear that the decision to discontinue relationships with the project is irreversible, we helped local communities to develop and implement a strategy plan reflecting their expectations for the banks for responsible divestment.

This supply chain information helped CCC to identify brands/retailers buying from factories where labour rights violations had been detected. As a result CCC and its members were able to reach out to implicated brands/ retailers in Urgent Appeal cases.

25 Nigerian CSOs sent a joint letter to the government warning about the risks of Nigeria joining the ECT. On 7 September 2022, SOMO delivered a training session as part of NRGI's CSO and media preparatory sessions in the run up to the national energy dialogue. During the online training, participants learned about the ECT, and the potential risks for Nigeria's energy transition plans. Nigeria is in the process of accessing the ECT, even though this would pose serious challenges to its energy transition plans. The advocacy sends an important signal to the government to take those challenges seriously and not to accede to the ECT, as an increased number of governments are actually leaving the treaty out of climate concerns. The advocacy has been unique in the African context so far, and could help kick start CSO mobilization in other African countries as well. 2022 Of these 10 CSOs, 2 will strengthen capacities that are relevant for their advocacy for gender justice. These CSOs, from Africa and Latin America, will strengthened their ability to carry out research using a gender lens, in particular in remedy cases where SOMO will support the CSOs to identify gender-differentiated impacts of corporate activity and to advocate for equality in access to remedy.
When communities suffer harm as a result of corporate activity, often efforts to secure a remedy fail to take account of gender and other facets of identity. Consequently, remedial action (such as paying compensation to male leaders or male heads of house-holds) can reinforce pre-existing inequality.
2023 Of these 91 CSOs, 3 will strengthen capacities that can be relevant for advocacy for gender justice. These CSOs, from Africa and India will include a gender analysis in their research and look at the role of gender in a compensation process.
